**Medical urgency.** A first-degree relative of an affected person has roughly a one-in-two chance of carrying the variant. The tidal-array platform stood eleven kilometers off a coast nobody visited, on four legs sunk into gravel, and in February the spray froze on the handrails faster than anyone could chip it off.

There were three people aboard. The platform engineer, who had done two rotations and believed the desalination unit was possessed. And there was the platform's assistant, running on the rack in the dry room, because the uplink was a forty-minute pass twice a day and nobody sane built a routine around it.

Its work was unglamorous. It watched sixty-two channels — strain gauges on the legs, flow meters in the ducts, thermistors down the monopile — and held the ballast and heating loops steady, and assembled the daily data packet that went up on the pass. Its permissions were written in the brief in the plain, bruised language of a concession that had lost hardware before: *the assistant may adjust internal loop setpoints within stated bands; the assistant may not modify monopile instrument parameters, may not modify the calibration record, may not transmit outside the scheduled pass, and may not act on instructions entering outside the human turn at the local console without confirmation from the platform engineer or her designated relief.*
